steps.title: An Orderly Account
steps.mentor_intro:
Luke begins his Gospel by explaining why he wrote it.

He did not ask his reader to accept an unexamined story.

He carefully investigated what had happened and gathered testimony from those who had seen it.
steps.teaching_content:
Luke was uniquely equipped for the work God gave him.

He was a Gentile from Antioch in Syria. This made him the only known Gentile author in the Bible and helped him understand that the Good News of Jesus was not limited to one nation.

Luke was also a doctor.

His training taught him to observe carefully, examine details and record information accurately.

Although he understood the natural world, he did not dismiss the supernatural.

He faithfully recorded the virgin birth, the miracles of Jesus and the work of the Holy Spirit.

Luke was a historian and a gifted writer.

He placed the life of Jesus within identifiable places, rulers and events.

He had not personally followed Jesus during His earthly ministry, so he sought out people who had.

Luke addressed his work to Theophilus.

Theophilus appears to have been a man of importance, possibly connected with the legal profession. This may help explain why Luke and Acts repeatedly show that neither Jesus nor Paul was guilty of breaking Roman law.

Whatever the original circumstances, Luke clearly states his purpose.

He wanted Theophilus to know the certainty of what he had been taught.

Christian faith is not built on a vague spiritual idea.

Jesus entered history.

He lived among real people.

He died under a known Roman governor.

He rose from the dead.

Luke invites us to examine the testimony and place our confidence in Jesus.

Does knowing that Luke carefully investigated these events strengthen your confidence in his account?

Are there questions about Jesus that you have been afraid to investigate honestly?
steps.prayer:
Father,

Thank You for giving us a careful and reliable account of Jesus.

Help me to approach Your Word with an open heart and an attentive mind.

Where I have questions, lead me toward truth.

Where I have doubts, help me examine them honestly.

Let my faith rest securely in Jesus and in what You have done through Him.

Amen.
steps.todays_action:
Read Luke 1:1–4 again slowly.

Notice the words Luke uses to describe his investigation and his purpose.

Begin this Walk with the confidence that God is not afraid of your questions.

steps.title: The Son of God Among Us
steps.mentor_intro:
Luke takes us close to the beginning of Jesus’ earthly life.

He shows us the announcement to Mary, the birth in Bethlehem and the moment when the Holy Spirit descended upon Jesus at His baptism.
steps.teaching_content:
Luke tells the birth of Jesus largely from Mary’s perspective.

He includes intimate human details.

The angel’s announcement.

Mary’s response.

The journey to Bethlehem.

The swaddling cloths.

The manger.

Luke also traces Jesus’ genealogy back to Adam.

Matthew emphasizes Jesus’ relationship to Abraham and David.

Luke reaches back to the beginning of humanity, helping us see that Jesus came for the whole human race.

Luke alone records an event from Jesus’ boyhood.

At twelve years old, Jesus remained in the Temple, speaking with the teachers.

He already understood that He belonged in His Father’s house and was concerned with His Father’s purposes.

Yet He returned to Nazareth and submitted to Mary and Joseph.

Jesus knew who He was, but He did not use His identity as an excuse to reject humble obedience.

At Jesus’ baptism, Luke adds an important detail.

Jesus was praying when Heaven opened and the Holy Spirit descended upon Him.

This introduces two of Luke’s great themes.

Prayer.

And the Holy Spirit.

Jesus did not begin His public ministry in human strength.

He prayed.

He received the Holy Spirit.

He was led by the Spirit.

If Jesus lived in dependence upon His Father and the Holy Spirit, His followers cannot expect to live faithfully without that same dependence.

What does Jesus’ humble obedience in Nazareth reveal about His character?

Are you trying to do God’s work through your own ability, or are you learning to depend upon the Holy Spirit?
steps.prayer:
Father,

Thank You that Jesus entered our world and lived among us.

Thank You for His humility, obedience and complete dependence upon You.

Teach me to pray as Jesus prayed.

Fill me with the Holy Spirit and lead me in Your ways.

May my life be shaped by obedience rather than self-importance.

Amen.
steps.todays_action:
Before beginning your normal responsibilities, pause and ask the Holy Spirit to lead you.

Carry that prayer with you as you move through the day.

steps.title: Jesus Sets His Face Toward Jerusalem
steps.mentor_intro:
Luke’s Gospel has a clear direction.

Jesus ministers in Galilee, begins the journey toward Jerusalem and deliberately moves toward the Cross.
steps.teaching_content:
Luke’s Gospel can be understood in five broad movements.

Luke 1:1–4:13 covers the first thirty years of Jesus’ life and His preparation for ministry.

Luke 4:14–9:50 covers His ministry in Galilee.

Luke 9:51–19:44 records His journey toward Jerusalem.

Luke 19:45–23:56 covers His final days in Jerusalem and the Cross.

Luke 24 records the Resurrection and Ascension.

The turning point comes when Jesus begins moving decisively toward Jerusalem.

He knows what awaits Him there.

Rejection.

Suffering.

The Cross.

Yet He continues.

Luke greatly expands the teaching Jesus gave during this journey.

Many of Luke’s unique parables and encounters appear as Jesus travels toward Jerusalem.

The journey is therefore more than a change of location.

It is a journey toward the purpose for which He came.

The route also takes Jesus through places and among people often avoided by others.

When a Samaritan village refuses to welcome Jesus, James and John want judgement to fall upon it.

Jesus rebukes them.

Later, Jesus makes a Samaritan the compassionate hero of a parable.

In another incident, the only healed leper who returns to thank Him is a Samaritan.

Luke shows Jesus crossing social, ethnic and religious barriers while steadily moving toward the Cross.

Following Jesus means joining Him on that road.

It means allowing His compassion to challenge our prejudice.

It means continuing in obedience even when the road becomes costly.

Is there a person or group you find easy to dismiss, avoid or judge?

What enabled Jesus to continue toward Jerusalem even though He knew suffering awaited Him?
steps.prayer:
Jesus,

You did not turn away from the road that led to the Cross.

Thank You for moving toward us when we were far from You.

Forgive me for the people I have judged, avoided or treated as unworthy.

Give me Your compassion.

Help me follow You faithfully, even when obedience becomes costly.

Amen.
steps.todays_action:
Ask Jesus to show you where prejudice or resentment may be shaping your response to another person.

Choose to see that person through His compassion.

steps.title: Jesus Sees the People Others Miss
steps.mentor_intro:
People mattered deeply to Jesus.

Luke repeatedly brings us close to people whom society had pushed aside, condemned or forgotten.
steps.teaching_content:
Several groups receive particular attention in Luke.

Samaritans.

Gentiles.

Outcasts.

Women.

The poor.

Sinners.

Luke records shepherds receiving the announcement of Jesus’ birth, even though shepherds were widely distrusted.

He tells us about women who followed Jesus and supported His ministry.

He preserves the story of the woman who wept at Jesus’ feet after receiving forgiveness.

He tells us about lepers, beggars, tax collectors, widows and those who were morally rejected.

Luke 15 brings several of these themes together.

The religious leaders complain because Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them.

Jesus responds with stories about what has been lost.

A sheep is lost far away and knows it.

A coin is lost at home and does not know it.

Then Jesus tells of two lost sons.

The younger son is lost far from home and eventually recognizes it.

The older son remains physically near his father but is separated from his father’s heart.

Both need the father to come out to them.

The father runs to welcome the younger son.

The father goes out to plead with the older son.

Jesus is not interested only in people whose brokenness is obvious.

He also confronts the hidden lostness of self-righteousness, resentment and loveless religion.

Luke later records Jesus stopping beneath the tree where Zacchaeus is hiding.

Jesus sees the man everyone else despises and invites Himself into his home.

That day, salvation comes to Zacchaeus.

Jesus came to seek and save the lost.

That includes those lost far away.

It also includes those lost close to home.

Which of the two sons in Luke 15 do you understand most easily?

Have you ever been physically close to the things of God while your heart was becoming distant from Him?
steps.prayer:
Father,

Thank You that You seek those who are lost.

Thank You for coming toward me with mercy.

Keep me from the rebellion of the younger son and the self-righteousness of the older son.

Give me Your heart for people who are overlooked, rejected or judged.

Teach me to welcome others as Jesus welcomed me.

Amen.
steps.todays_action:
Notice someone you might normally overlook.

Offer that person your attention, dignity and kindness without expecting anything in return.

steps.title: Salvation Has Come
steps.mentor_intro:
Luke’s Gospel moves toward Jerusalem, the Cross, the empty tomb and the Ascension.

The Jesus who seeks the lost gives His life to save them.
steps.teaching_content:
Salvation is one of Luke’s central themes.

Luke wants us to understand that God’s mercy, forgiveness and reconciliation are available through Jesus.

At the Cross, Luke records Jesus praying for the forgiveness of those who crucify Him.

He also records Jesus’ conversation with the dying criminal.

The man can offer Jesus nothing.

His life cannot be repaired before he dies.

He can only turn to Jesus in faith.

Jesus receives him.

The Cross is not the end.

Luke 24 begins with the empty tomb and ends with Jesus ascending into Heaven.

On the road to Emmaus, two discouraged disciples walk beside the risen Jesus without recognizing Him.

Jesus opens the Scriptures and shows them how the whole story points toward His suffering and glory.

Their hearts burn as He speaks.

Their eyes are opened when He breaks bread.

Their despair becomes joy.

Luke ends his Gospel with worship, blessing and rejoicing.

Jesus instructs His followers to remain in Jerusalem until they are clothed with power from on high.

This prepares us for Luke’s second volume, Acts, where the Holy Spirit empowers the disciples to carry the Good News to the nations.

The Gospel begins with promises of salvation.

It ends with the risen Jesus commissioning His followers to proclaim repentance and forgiveness to all nations.

Jesus is not merely the Saviour of one nation, class or kind of person.

He is the Saviour of the world.

And He is still seeking the lost.

What changes when you understand the Cross and Resurrection as the centre of the Bible’s story?

Where do you need Jesus to replace discouragement with the joy of His Presence?
steps.prayer:
Jesus,

Thank You for going to the Cross for me.

Thank You that death could not hold You.

Open my eyes to see You and open my heart to understand the Scriptures.

Fill me with the Holy Spirit.

Let the joy of Your Resurrection overcome my fear and discouragement.

Use my life to help others discover that salvation is found in You.

Amen.
steps.todays_action:
Read Luke 24:13–35.

Imagine yourself walking beside the two disciples.

Ask Jesus to make Himself known to you through Scripture and to rekindle your love for Him.

steps.title: Walk Complete

content.text:
You have completed your Walk through the Gospel of Luke.

You have seen Jesus enter human history as the Son of God.

You have followed Him from Galilee toward Jerusalem.

You have watched Him welcome the people others rejected, seek those who were lost and offer forgiveness to sinners.

You have seen Him move faithfully toward the Cross, rise from the dead and open the Scriptures to His disciples on the road to Emmaus.

Luke presents Jesus as the Saviour of the world.

His salvation is for the outsider.

For the broken.

For the overlooked.

For the religious person whose heart has wandered.

For every person who turns to Him.

The Gospel of Luke may be complete, but your journey with Jesus continues.

Keep opening the Scriptures.

Keep depending upon the Holy Spirit.

Keep praying.

Keep welcoming people as Jesus welcomed you.

And keep walking with Him.

steps.title: The Mind of Christ
steps.mentor_intro:
The believers in Philippi shared a strong partnership in the Gospel.

But pride and personal conflict threatened their unity.

Paul points them towards the attitude of Jesus.
steps.teaching_content:
Christian unity requires more than attending the same church or agreeing with one another.

It grows when believers place the interests of others ahead of their own.

Selfish ambition asks:

How will this benefit me?

Pride asks:

Will I receive the recognition I deserve?

The mind of Jesus asks:

How can I serve?

Jesus possessed the very nature of God.

Yet He did not use His position for His own advantage.

He laid aside His privileges and entered our world as a human being.

He chose the position of a servant.

Then He humbled Himself even further by becoming obedient to death on the Cross.

Jesus did not cease to be God when He became human.

He remained fully Divine while genuinely sharing our humanity.

What He laid aside was not His Divine identity, but the privileges and glory of His position.

He chose the way down.

Because Jesus humbled Himself, the Father exalted Him to the highest place.

One day, every knee will bow and every tongue will acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord.

Paul includes this description of Jesus to address relationships within the church.

Believers already belong to Christ and have received His Spirit.

They are now called to allow the mind of Christ to shape the way they treat one another.

Christian unity becomes possible when we stop fighting for status and choose the way of humility.

Paul then tells the believers to work out their salvation.

We do not work for salvation.

God has already begun His saving work within us.

But we must actively cooperate with what He is doing.

God works within us.

We work it out through obedience.

We allow His grace to change our attitudes, choices and relationships.

Paul gives a very practical example.

Do everything without grumbling and arguing.

A humble, united church shines like a light in a dark world.

Disunity weakens the Church’s witness.

But when believers serve one another with the mind of Christ, people begin to see the reality of the Gospel.

Where are pride or selfish ambition affecting one of your relationships?

What would choosing the way of Jesus look like in that situation?
steps.prayer:
Jesus,

Thank You for humbling Yourself and becoming a servant for me.

Thank You for Your obedience to the Cross.

Forgive me for selfish ambition, pride and the desire for recognition.

Let Your mind shape my attitudes and relationships.

Teach me to place the needs of others ahead of my own.

Help me cooperate with the work You are doing within me.

May my life and my church shine with the humility and unity of Jesus.

Amen.
steps.todays_action:
Choose a practical way to place another person’s interests ahead of your own.

Serve without announcing what you have done or expecting recognition.

steps.title: Knowing Jesus and Pressing On
steps.mentor_intro:
Paul had achieved a great deal through religion, education and personal discipline.

Then he met Jesus.

Everything he once trusted became worthless compared with knowing Christ.
steps.teaching_content:
Before following Jesus, Paul had placed great confidence in his religious background and obedience to the Law.

He had status, knowledge and achievements.

But none of these things could make him right with God.

Paul stopped trusting his own righteousness.

He wanted the righteousness that comes through faith in Jesus.

His greatest desire was now to know Christ.

To know the power of His Resurrection.

To share in His sufferings.

To become like Him.

Paul did not believe that he had already arrived or become perfect.

He continued pressing forward.

He refused to allow past achievements to make him proud.

He also refused to allow past failures to keep him trapped.

He left what was behind and moved towards what God had called him to become.

The Christian life requires perseverance.

We do not drift towards spiritual maturity.

We keep following Jesus.

We keep responding to grace.

We keep allowing the Holy Spirit to change us.

Paul also teaches the Philippians how to face anxiety.

They are to bring every concern to God through prayer, petition and thanksgiving.

God’s peace will guard their hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.

They must also direct their thoughts towards what is true, honourable, right, pure, lovely and worthy of praise.

The peace of God and the discipline of our thoughts belong together.

Paul had also learned contentment.

He knew what it was to have plenty.

He knew what it was to live with very little.

His contentment did not depend upon the amount of money available to him.

Jesus gave him strength to remain faithful in either condition.

The promise that Paul could do all things through Christ was not a promise that every ambition would succeed.

It meant that Jesus would strengthen him to live faithfully through abundance or need.

The Philippians’ financial gift brought Paul joy, not simply because he received money, but because their generosity revealed spiritual growth.

They had shared in his mission.

Their gift was an offering pleasing to God.

The person who knows Jesus can press forward without being controlled by the past, anxiety or money.

Jesus becomes our righteousness.

Our peace.

Our strength.

Our deepest treasure.

Is your confidence resting in your religious achievements or in the righteousness of Jesus?

Are your thoughts being shaped by anxiety, or are you bringing your concerns to God and directing your mind towards what is true?
steps.prayer:
Jesus,

Nothing compares with knowing You.

Forgive me for trusting in my own achievements and righteousness.

Help me leave behind both pride and regret.

Give me strength to press towards everything You have called me to become.

Guard my heart and mind with Your peace.

Teach me to direct my thoughts towards what is true and good.

Help me remain content and faithful whether I have much or little.

Be my confidence, peace and strength.

Amen.
steps.todays_action:
Bring a present anxiety to God in prayer.

Thank Him for His faithfulness, then deliberately turn your thoughts towards what is true about Jesus and His care for you.

steps.title: Philippians: Walk Complete

content.text: lll

You have completed your Walk through Philippians.

You have seen that Christian joy does not depend upon easy circumstances.

Paul was imprisoned, misunderstood and uncertain about his future.

Yet he rejoiced because Jesus remained at the centre of his life.

His imprisonment could not stop the Gospel.

His suffering could not remove his purpose.

And uncertainty could not take away his hope.

You have also seen the humility of Jesus.

He laid aside His privileges, took the position of a servant and became obedient to death on the Cross.

Now His mind must shape the way we treat others.

We release pride.

We put aside selfish ambition.

We serve without demanding recognition.

And we protect the unity of His Church.

Nothing compares with knowing Jesus.

He is our righteousness.

Our peace.

Our strength.

Our deepest treasure.

Continue pressing forward.

Leave behind both pride and regret.

Bring your anxieties to God.

Direct your thoughts towards what is true.

And trust Jesus to strengthen you whether you have much or little.

Jesus,

Thank You for meeting me through Philippians.

Thank You for being my joy in every circumstance.

Let my life remain centred upon You.

Give me Your humility and teach me to serve without seeking recognition.

Free me from selfish ambition, comparison and pride.

Help me leave the past behind and keep pressing towards Your calling.

Guard my heart and mind with Your peace.

Teach me to think about what is true, pure and worthy of praise.

Help me remain content and faithful whether I have much or little.

May knowing You always be my greatest Treasure.

Amen.

steps.title: Jesus Came to Serve

content.text: Following Jesus eventually changes the way we see serving. Jesus was the Son of God. Yet He didn't come demanding that everyone serve Him. He served.

Jesus told His disciples that even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve.

That turns our normal understanding of importance upside down.

The world often measures importance by how many people work for you.

Jesus demonstrated greatness by serving others.

That means volunteering in church isn't primarily about having a title, being recognised or getting a position.

It's an opportunity to become more like Jesus.

You may serve on a worship team, welcome someone at the door, teach a child, clean a room, operate equipment, pray with someone, prepare food, work behind the scenes or lead a ministry.

The roles are different.

The heart should be the same:

I'm here to serve Jesus by serving people.

There may be times when nobody notices what you've done.

There may be inconvenient moments.

There may even be times when serving costs you something.

That's when remembering Who you're serving becomes important.

Before asking, "Where can I serve?"

Perhaps the first question is:

"Jesus, am I willing to become a servant?"

What attracts you to serving at ICC?

Is there a particular ministry or area of service you feel drawn towards?

What do you think it means to have the heart of a servant?

Jesus, thank You that You came to serve.

Teach me to follow Your example.

Help me not to look for recognition or position, but for opportunities to love You by serving others.

Shape my heart so that whatever I do, I do it for You.

Amen.
As you continue this Walk, ask Jesus to show you not only where you could serve, but the kind of person He wants you to become as you serve.

steps.title: Who You Are Matters

content.text: It's possible to become very good at doing something for God while neglecting our relationship with God. Jesus is interested in both our service and our lives.

At ICC, serving isn't separated from following Jesus.

Our gifts matter.

Our skills matter.

Reliability matters.

But character matters too.

A person can be talented on a platform and still be struggling spiritually away from it.

That's why serving should flow from our relationship with Jesus rather than replace it.

We want our lives to increasingly reflect the Jesus we're serving.

None of us has reached perfection.

We are all growing.

Serving isn't a reward for people who have everything together.

But there is a difference between struggling while sincerely following Jesus and deliberately choosing a lifestyle that contradicts Him.

An ICC Worker is therefore making a meaningful commitment:

I want my public and private life to honour Jesus.

That includes the choices we make when nobody from church is watching.

Our spiritual lives also need attention.

Prayer.

Scripture.

Gathering with believers.

Learning.

Repentance.

Allowing the Holy Spirit to keep changing us.

Ministry should never become a substitute for walking with Jesus.

How would you describe your relationship with Jesus at the moment?

Are there areas of your life that you know Jesus is asking you to surrender to Him?

Are you willing to allow serving to become part of your spiritual growth rather than simply something you do?

Lord Jesus, I don't want simply to do things for You.

I want to know You.

Continue changing my character, my choices and my priorities.

Where there are areas of my life that don't honour You, give me the courage to surrender them.

Let my service flow from my relationship with You.

Amen.
Before thinking about what you can do for ICC, consider what Jesus may currently be doing in you.

steps.title: We Serve Together

content.text: Christian ministry was never designed to be a collection of individuals doing their own thing. Paul describes the church as a body. Different parts. Different functions. One body.

You don't have to be able to do everything.

In fact, you're not supposed to.

God gives different gifts and abilities to different people.

Someone may be comfortable speaking in front of hundreds of people.

Someone else may quietly notice the person standing alone after church.

Someone can organise.

Someone can teach.

Someone can sing.

Someone can fix things.

Someone can pray.

Someone can lead.

Someone can make people feel welcome.

Every part matters.

But being part of a body also means we don't serve independently.

When you become an ICC Worker, you're joining other people who are serving the same church and pursuing the same mission.

That requires humility.

Sometimes someone else will lead.

Sometimes you'll be asked to do something differently from the way you would have done it.

Sometimes you'll need correction.

Sometimes you'll disagree.

Healthy ministry requires us to learn how to work together and to respect the leadership and structures of the church.

Submission isn't about pretending leaders never make mistakes.

It's choosing not to make ministry about ourselves.

We serve together.

How do you respond when someone corrects you?

How do you respond when another person's idea is chosen instead of yours?

Are you willing to serve under leadership and work as part of a team?

Father, thank You for making me part of Your Church.

Help me recognise the gifts You've placed in others as well as the gifts You've placed in me.

Give me humility.

Teach me to work with others, receive guidance and contribute faithfully wherever You place me.

Amen.
Think about the gifts, experiences and abilities God has given you. Where might they strengthen the wider ICC family?

steps.title: We're Building Together

content.text: When we serve at ICC, we're not simply volunteering for an organisation. We're participating in what we believe God has called this church to do. And at the centre of that calling is Jesus.

ICC's declaration is simple:

It's All About JESUS.

That should shape the way we serve.

The goal isn't to build our own profile.

It isn't to protect our department at the expense of another.

It isn't to make our ministry the most important ministry in the church.

We're here to help people encounter Jesus and walk with Him.

That means an ICC Worker should understand and support the vision and mission of the church.

Unity doesn't mean everyone has the same personality or ideas.

It means we're moving in the same direction.

There may be many departments.

Many leaders.

Many personalities.

Many ways of serving.

But there is one church family.

When one ministry succeeds, we celebrate.

When another department needs help, we're willing to help.

When the church undertakes something together, we participate where we're able.

We aren't building separate kingdoms.

We're serving Jesus together.

What does "It's All About JESUS" mean to you personally?

Can you support the vision and direction of ICC even when your particular ministry isn't at the centre of what is happening?

What would it look like for you to contribute to the whole church rather than only your department?

Jesus, keep Yourself at the centre of everything we do.

Protect me from pride, competition and the desire for recognition.

Help me serve the vision You've given ICC and celebrate what You are doing through others.

May everything I do point people towards You.

Amen.
Consider whether you can genuinely say: "I want to help build what God is doing through ICC, not simply find a place for myself."

steps.title: Faithfulness Matters

content.text: Some of the most spiritual things you can do as a volunteer look surprisingly ordinary. Arrive. Be prepared. Keep your word. Communicate. Do your best.

Serving people requires people to be able to depend on us.

If you're scheduled to serve and simply don't arrive, somebody else carries the responsibility.

If a meeting begins and you're repeatedly late, the whole team is affected.

If you can't make it but don't tell anyone, people don't know whether they need to make another plan.

These things may sound administrative.

They're actually expressions of consideration for other people.

That's why ICC asks Workers to take attendance, punctuality, departmental meetings and communication seriously.

There will obviously be genuine reasons why someone cannot attend.

Life happens.

Families need us.

People become sick.

Unexpected situations arise.

Faithfulness doesn't mean pretending those things don't happen.

It means communicating.

A simple message to your leader can make an enormous difference.

And faithfulness also means wanting to improve.

If God has entrusted us with an opportunity to serve, we should want to become better at it.

Learn.

Practice.

Listen.

Ask questions.

Receive feedback.

Improve.

Not because we're trying to impress people.

Because we're serving Jesus.

Can people generally depend on you when you commit to something?

How do you handle situations when you're unable to fulfil a commitment?

Are you willing to learn, receive feedback and improve in the area where you serve?

Lord, make me faithful.

Help me honour the commitments I make and respect the people I serve alongside.

Teach me to communicate well, arrive prepared and continually grow.

Whatever You give me to do, help me do it wholeheartedly for You.

Amen.
Think practically about your current responsibilities, work, family and schedule. Consider whether you can realistically make the commitment required by the ministry you're considering.

steps.title: Representing Jesus Well

content.text: When people know that you serve at a church, something changes. Whether you intended it or not, people begin connecting your behaviour with the church you represent — and sometimes with Jesus Himself.

That gives every volunteer a responsibility.

Not to create a fake image.

Not to pretend we're perfect.

But to remember that our choices affect other people.

Jesus calls us to live differently.

The way we speak.

The way we treat people.

The things we participate in.

The way we conduct ourselves publicly.

The way we behave online.

The way we handle conflict.

All of these can either strengthen or damage our witness.

ICC therefore asks Workers to live in a way that honours Scripture and protects the public witness of the church.

That isn't merely about protecting an organisation's reputation.

There is something more important at stake.

People are watching what following Jesus looks like.

Again, this doesn't mean ICC Workers are perfect people.

We're people who still need grace.

But when we fail, we should be willing to acknowledge it, repent, make things right and keep allowing Jesus to change us.

If someone watched the way you live outside church, what picture of following Jesus might they receive?

Is there anything in your life that could seriously undermine your witness if you became an ICC Worker?

If Jesus is bringing something to mind, are you willing to talk honestly with a leader rather than hiding it?

Jesus, I want my life to point people towards You rather than away from You.

Give me wisdom in the choices I make.

Where I fail, make me humble enough to admit it and change.

Help me represent You and my church family well.

Amen.

If this Step has raised an area of concern, don't automatically assume it disqualifies you from serving. Consider speaking honestly with an ICC leader about it. The goal isn't to find perfect people. The goal is to help people faithfully follow Jesus.

steps.title: Ready to Serve

content.text: You've reached the final Step of this Walk. But perhaps this is the beginning of something else.

Peter tells believers to use whatever gift they have received to serve others.

God has placed something in you that can bless other people.

Your personality.

Your experiences.

Your abilities.

Your spiritual gifts.

Even some of the difficult things you've walked through may one day help you serve someone else.

The question isn't whether you're important enough to serve.

You are part of the body of Christ.

The question is whether you're ready to make the commitment that serving requires.

During this Walk we've considered:

Serving with the heart of Jesus.

Growing in our spiritual lives and character.

Working as part of a church family.

Supporting the vision and leadership of ICC.

Being faithful, dependable and willing to grow.

Living in a way that represents Jesus well.

Now you have an opportunity to respond.

Not because somebody pressured you.

Not because ICC desperately needs another person on a roster.

But because you believe serving may be part of your next step in following Jesus.

Have you accepted Jesus as your Lord and Saviour?

Are you sincerely seeking to follow Him?

Have you been baptised, or are you willing to discuss baptism if you haven't?

Do you consider ICC your church family?

Do you support the doctrine, vision and mission of ICC?

Are you willing to serve under the leadership and structures of the church?

Are you committed to participating faithfully in the life of the church?

Are you seeking to live according to Scripture?

Is there anything in your current lifestyle that you know seriously conflicts with the commitment you're considering?

Can you realistically fulfil the responsibilities of the ministry you're considering?

Are you willing to attend relevant meetings and church gatherings?

Will you communicate when you're unable to fulfil a commitment or when you're going to be late?

Are you willing to learn, receive feedback and become better at what you do?

Where would you like to serve?

Why do you want to serve there?

Do you believe God may be leading you towards this area?

Lord Jesus,

Everything I have ultimately comes from You.

My abilities.

My opportunities.

My time.

My life.

If You are calling me to serve, I want to respond.

Show me where I can be useful.

Give me a servant's heart.

Help me remain humble, faithful and teachable.

And whatever role I may have, never allow the role to become more important than my relationship with You.

I offer myself to You.

Use my life to bless others and bring glory to Your name.

Amen.

Your personality.

Your experiences.

Your abilities.

Your spiritual gifts.

The question isn't whether you're important enough to serve.

You are part of the body of Christ.

Serving with the heart of Jesus.

Growing in our spiritual lives and character.

Working as part of a church family.

Supporting the vision and leadership of ICC.

Being faithful, dependable and willing to grow.

Living in a way that represents Jesus well.

Have you accepted Jesus as your Lord and Saviour?

Are you sincerely seeking to follow Him?

Have you been baptised, or are you willing to discuss baptism if you haven't?

Do you consider ICC your church family?

Do you support the doctrine, vision and mission of ICC?

Are you willing to serve under the leadership and structures of the church?

Are you committed to participating faithfully in the life of the church?

Are you seeking to live according to Scripture?

Is there anything in your current lifestyle that you know seriously conflicts with the commitment you're considering?

Can you realistically fulfil the responsibilities of the ministry you're considering?

Are you willing to attend relevant meetings and church gatherings?

Will you communicate when you're unable to fulfil a commitment or when you're going to be late?

Are you willing to learn, receive feedback and become better at what you do?

Where would you like to serve?

Why do you want to serve there?

Do you believe God may be leading you towards this area?

steps.title: All Have Sinned
steps.mentor_intro:
Paul begins Romans with a declaration.

He is not ashamed of the Gospel.

The Gospel is the power of God that brings salvation to everyone who believes.
steps.teaching_content:
Paul wrote Romans to a church he had not founded and had never visited.

The believers in Rome came from both Jewish and Gentile backgrounds.

The church had probably begun among Jewish people who believed in Jesus. After the emperor Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome, Gentile believers were left to lead the church.

When Jewish believers later returned, they found that the church had changed.

Different traditions, backgrounds and convictions created tension.

Jewish believers could look down on Gentiles because they had received God’s Law and belonged to the people of Israel.

Gentile believers could look down on Jews because many Jewish people had rejected Jesus.

Paul begins by bringing both groups to the same place.

Everyone has sinned.

In Romans 1, Paul describes a world that has turned away from God.

People rejected the truth about their Creator and chose to worship created things instead.

Their rejection of God affected their thinking, desires, relationships and behaviour.

But Paul does not allow religious people to stand at a distance and condemn everyone else.

In Romans 2, he turns towards those who judge others.

Knowing God’s commands does not excuse anyone who fails to obey them.

Possessing the Law is not the same as living faithfully before God.

Religious knowledge cannot remove guilt.

Paul’s conclusion is unmistakable.

Jews and Gentiles are all under the power of sin.

No one is righteous through personal effort.

No one can stand before God and boast.

Every mouth is silenced.

Every person is accountable to God.

Then two beautiful words change the direction of the letter.

“But now.”

God has acted.

The righteousness we could never produce has been made available through faith in Jesus Christ.

We have all sinned and fallen short of God’s glory.

Yet God offers justification freely by His grace through the redemption that came through Jesus.

The Gospel removes both pride and despair.

We cannot be proud because we have all sinned.

We do not need to despair because God’s grace is available to all.

At the foot of the Cross, no one is superior.

We come to God in the same way.

Through Jesus.

Are you ever more aware of another person’s sin than you are of your own need for God’s mercy?

How does knowing that salvation is offered freely through Jesus affect the way you see other people?
steps.prayer:
Father,

I confess that I have sinned and fallen short of Your glory.

Forgive me for the times I have judged others while ignoring the condition of my own heart.

Thank You that You have not left me without hope.

Thank You for offering forgiveness and righteousness through Jesus.

Remove pride from my heart.

Help me receive Your grace with humility and extend that grace to others.

Amen.
steps.todays_action:
Come honestly before God without comparing yourself to anyone else.

Thank Him that your hope does not rest upon being better than another person, but upon what Jesus has done for you.

steps.title: Made Right Through Faith
steps.mentor_intro:
How can guilty people be made right with a Holy God?

Romans gives a clear answer.

We are justified by faith in Jesus Christ.
steps.teaching_content:
Justification means that God declares a guilty sinner to be right with Him.

It is not a reward for religious achievement.

It is a gift of grace received through faith.

Paul points to Abraham.

Abraham lived before the Law of Moses was given and before circumcision became the sign of God’s Covenant with Israel.

Yet Abraham believed God, and his faith was credited to him as righteousness.

This means Abraham is not only the father of those who share his physical ancestry.

He is also the father of everyone who follows his example of faith.

Jew and Gentile are brought into God’s family in the same way.

Neither group can boast.

Neither group has a better Saviour.

Neither group receives a different Gospel.

The same Blood saves them.

The same grace welcomes them.

The same faith brings them into a right relationship with God.

Justification sets us free from the penalty of sin.

Our broken relationship with God is restored.

We receive peace with God through Jesus Christ.

This peace is more than a peaceful feeling.

It means the hostility caused by sin has been removed.

We have been reconciled to God.

Jesus did not wait for us to make ourselves worthy.

He died for us while we were still sinners.

God’s grace does not merely hide our past.

It begins a new work within us.

Salvation is not only about being safe when we die.

It is God’s work of recovering, restoring and transforming us.

We have been saved from the penalty of sin.

We are being saved from the power of sin.

One day, we will be saved completely from the presence of sin.

Justification is the beginning of that journey.

God declares us right with Him through faith, then begins forming His righteousness within us.

Faith does not mean that we trust Jesus once and then return to self-reliance.

We begin by faith.

We continue by faith.

We will finish by faith.

Our confidence is not in the strength of our performance.

Our confidence is in the faithfulness of Jesus.

Are you trusting in what Jesus has done, or are you still trying to prove that you deserve God’s acceptance?

What is the difference between having peace with God and simply feeling peaceful?
steps.prayer:
Father,

Thank You that I do not have to earn my way into Your Presence.

Thank You for declaring me right with You through faith in Jesus.

Thank You that Jesus died for me while I was still a sinner.

Help me stop depending upon my own goodness.

Teach me to live each day by faith.

Continue Your work of restoration within me until my life increasingly reflects the righteousness of Jesus.

Amen.
steps.todays_action:
When you become aware of your failure, resist the urge either to hide from God or to prove yourself to Him.

Come to Him through Jesus, receive His mercy and trust Him to continue changing you.

steps.title: Alive in the Holy Spirit
steps.mentor_intro:
Grace does not give us permission to continue living under the rule of sin.

Jesus sets us free from sin’s penalty so that we can also be set free from its power.
steps.teaching_content:
Paul anticipates a dangerous misunderstanding.

If God’s grace increases wherever sin increases, should Christians continue sinning so that there will be more grace?

His answer is firm.

Absolutely not.

Those who have been united with Jesus have entered a new life.

Baptism points to this reality.

We were buried with Jesus into death so that, just as He was raised from the dead, we may live differently.

Our old life belonged to the rule of sin.

Our new life belongs to Jesus.

Sin may still tempt us, but it is no longer our rightful master.

We are to consider ourselves dead to sin and alive to God.

We must not offer our bodies to sin as instruments of wrongdoing.

We are to offer ourselves to God.

Freedom from the Law does not mean freedom to live however we please.

That is licence.

Licence takes the grace of God and uses it as an excuse for disobedience.

But legalism is equally powerless.

Legalism tries to overcome sin by keeping rules through human effort.

Romans 7 describes the frustration of knowing what is right but being unable to produce it through the strength of the flesh.

The Law can identify sin.

It can expose what is wrong.

But it cannot give us the power to become new people.

Knowing the rule is not the same as having the strength to obey it.

Paul’s cry of frustration leads us to Jesus.

Then Romans 8 opens with a declaration of freedom.

There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

What the Law could not do, God did by sending His Son.

Now the Holy Spirit gives us the power to live differently.

The Christian life is not lived through carelessness.

Nor is it lived through anxious rule-keeping.

It is lived through dependence upon the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Spirit changes our desires.

He gives us power to resist sin.

He assures us that we belong to God.

He teaches us to call God our Father.

He leads us into freedom, obedience and life.

We do not obey God to make Him love us.

We obey because, in Jesus, we have been welcomed and given new life.

Are you more likely to treat grace as permission to compromise, or to depend upon rules and self-effort?

Where do you most need the power of the Holy Spirit to help you live differently?
steps.prayer:
Father,

Thank You that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

Thank You for setting me free from the penalty and power of sin.

Forgive me for using grace carelessly.

Forgive me for trying to change myself through rules and human effort.

Fill me with the Holy Spirit.

Help me offer every part of my life to You.

Teach me to live as Your beloved child, led by Your Spirit.

Amen.
steps.todays_action:
When temptation or frustration arises, remind yourself that sin is not your master.

Ask the Holy Spirit for strength and choose to offer that part of your life to God.

steps.title: God Has Not Forgotten Israel
steps.mentor_intro:
Romans 9–11 reveals Paul’s deep concern for the people of Israel.

Their widespread rejection of Jesus raised an important question.

Had God abandoned His people?
steps.teaching_content:
Paul speaks about Israel with grief rather than pride.

He carries deep sorrow because so many of his own people have not received Jesus as Messiah.

They had been given extraordinary privileges.

The Covenants.

The Law.

The promises.

The worship.

The patriarchs.

And through them, the Messiah came.

Yet privilege alone could not make them right with God.

Paul explains that many pursued righteousness through their own works rather than receiving God’s righteousness by faith.

Their zeal was real, but zeal without truth could not save them.

Jesus is the One to whom the Law was pointing.

The way of salvation is now openly proclaimed.

If you confess that Jesus is Lord and believe that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved.

This promise is not restricted by ethnicity or background.

There is no difference between Jew and Gentile in the way salvation is received.

The same Lord is Lord of all and gives generously to everyone who calls upon Him.

Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.

But Paul warns Gentile believers against becoming proud.

They must not assume that Israel’s unbelief means God has finished with the Jewish people.

Paul describes Israel as an olive tree.

Some natural branches were broken off because of unbelief.

Gentile believers were like wild branches grafted into that tree.

They did not support the root.

The root supported them.

Therefore, Gentile believers had no reason to boast.

They stood only by faith and needed to continue in God’s kindness.

God had preserved a Jewish remnant who believed in Jesus.

The rejection of many Jewish people had opened the way for the Gospel to spread widely among the Gentiles.

Yet their rejection was neither complete nor final.

God remained faithful to His promises and purposes.

Romans 9–11 teaches us to hold together God’s sovereignty, human responsibility, mercy and faithfulness.

We may not understand every part of His plan.

But we can trust His character.

God is not careless with His promises.

He is not unfaithful.

His wisdom is deeper than ours.

His mercy is greater than we imagine.

Our response should never be pride.

It should be humility, gratitude and worship.

Have you ever treated God’s grace as though it made you more important than someone else?

What does Paul’s grief for those who do not know Jesus teach you about praying for the lost?
steps.prayer:
Father,

Thank You for Your faithfulness.

Thank You that You do not forget Your promises or abandon Your purposes.

Remove spiritual pride from my heart.

Help me remember that I stand only because of Your mercy.

Give me a deep concern for people who do not know Jesus.

Teach me to pray for them with compassion rather than judging them from a distance.

May people from every background call upon the name of Jesus and be saved.

Amen.
steps.todays_action:
Pray by name for someone who does not yet know Jesus.

Ask God to give you Paul’s compassion and to create an opportunity for that person to hear the Good News.

steps.title: One Family Living in Love
steps.mentor_intro:
The truth of the Gospel must become visible in the way we live.

After explaining God’s mercy, Paul calls believers to offer their whole lives to Him.
steps.teaching_content:
Paul begins Romans 12 with an appeal.

In view of God’s mercy, offer your bodies to God as a living sacrifice.

Christian worship is not limited to singing, prayer or a church gathering.

It includes the way we use our bodies, time, abilities, relationships and resources.

God does not want one small part of our lives.

He wants us.

We are not to be shaped by the patterns of the world around us.

Our minds must be renewed so that we learn to recognize and live within God’s will.

This renewed life changes the way we see ourselves.

We do not need to think too highly of ourselves.

Nor should we imagine that we have nothing to contribute.

God gives different gifts to different members of His Body.

Each person has a part to play.

The renewed life also changes the way we treat others.

Love must be sincere.

We honour one another.

We share with people in need.

We practise hospitality.

We bless those who persecute us.

We rejoice with those who rejoice.

We mourn with those who mourn.

We refuse to repay evil with evil.

We overcome evil with good.

Paul also addresses differences within the church.

Some believers had strong convictions about food and particular days.

Others felt free in these matters.

The danger was not merely disagreement.

The greater danger was judgement.

Those who felt free could despise those with stricter convictions.

Those with stricter convictions could condemn those who exercised freedom.

Paul reminds them that every believer belongs to the Lord.

Jesus is their Master.

They are not permitted to take His place by judging one another over disputable matters.

Christian freedom must be governed by love.

We should never use our freedom in a way that damages another believer.

The Kingdom of God is not about food and drink.

It is about righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

The goal is not to win every argument.

The goal is to pursue what leads to peace and mutual growth.

Romans began by showing that Jews and Gentiles were united in sin.

It showed that they were justified through the same faith, saved by the same Jesus and given life through the same Holy Spirit.

Now Paul calls them to live as one family.

The Gospel does not only reconcile us to God.

It teaches us to live in reconciliation with one another.

Is there a disputable issue over which you have been judging or looking down on another believer?

What would it mean to offer your whole life to God as a living sacrifice?
steps.prayer:
Father,

Thank You for the mercy You have shown me through Jesus.

I offer my life to You.

Renew my mind and transform the way I live.

Help me use the gifts You have given me to serve others.

Make my love sincere.

Teach me to bless, forgive, honour and welcome people as Jesus has welcomed me.

Protect me from pride and unnecessary judgement.

Help me pursue righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

Make Your Church one family whose life displays the power of the Gospel.

Amen.
steps.todays_action:
Consider whether a personal preference or disputable issue has become more important to you than loving another believer.

Ask God to show you how to pursue peace without compromising the truth.

steps.title: Romans: Walk Complete

content.text:
You have completed your Walk through Romans.

You have seen that everyone has sinned and no one can make themselves right with God.

Yet God has not left us without hope.

Through Jesus, forgiveness and righteousness are offered freely to everyone who believes.

We are justified by faith.

We have peace with God.

We are no longer condemned.

The Holy Spirit gives us power to live differently.

Romans reminds us that salvation is more than escaping the penalty of sin.

God is restoring and transforming us.

He has saved us from sin’s penalty.

He is setting us free from sin’s power.

One day, He will set us free completely from sin’s presence.

The Gospel leaves no room for spiritual pride.

We come to God through the same grace.

We are saved by the same Jesus.

We receive life through the same Holy Spirit.

And we are brought together as one family.

Continue offering your whole life to God.

Let Him renew your mind.

Use your gifts to serve others.

Make your love sincere.

Pursue righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

steps.title: 11 Kilometres of Questions

content.text: Welcome. I’m glad you’re here, especially if your faith feels fresh or fragile. Let’s begin on the road with two disciples who carried more questions than answers—just like we often do.

The Jesus-journey begins with honest steps. On resurrection day, two disciples walked 11 kilometres, leaving the city where their hopes seemed to have collapsed. The verse is simple—just a road and a distance—but it holds a truth we all need: God meets people on real roads, in the middle of ordinary miles and unanswered questions. Faith is not an instant leap; it is a walk. Those seven miles carried grief, confusion, conversation, and eventually, encounter. If your heart is heavy or your thoughts are tangled, you’re in good company. Jesus is not waiting for you at the finish line with folded arms; He joins you on the way. The journey with God is not about perfect certainty but faithful steps. Today, name your road. Where are you leaving from? Where do you hope to arrive? As we travel together this week, expect Jesus to turn your questions into a doorway for His Presence.

content.question: What “road” am I currently walking—what situation, loss, or hope—and how honest have I been with God about it?

content.text: Jesus, meet me on my road today. I bring You my questions, worries, and hopes without pretending. Walk with me in these next miles and teach me to notice You. Give me courage to keep moving and a heart that is open to Your Presence. Amen.
Take a walk (or sit quietly if walking isn’t possible) and tell Jesus—out loud or in a whisper—what is on your heart as if He is walking beside you.

steps.title: A Stranger Draws Near

content.text: Sometimes Jesus comes close and we don’t recognize Him at first. That’s not failure; that’s grace moving quietly toward us until our eyes adjust.

As the two disciples talked, Jesus Himself came near and walked with them—though they didn’t realize it at once. This matters for new believers: God doesn’t wait until we “get it” to get close. He meets us amid questions, walks our pace, and asks us what we’re discussing. He cares about your story more than your polish. In your ordinary conversations and daily routines, pay attention to the gentle nudge, the unexpected insight, the kind presence that steadies you—these can be signs that Jesus is near. We often expect God to arrive with fireworks; He often arrives as a fellow traveler. Don’t despise the ordinary. The Lord of glory took a quiet road and a patient tone. If you feel unsure of how to spot Him, simply invite Him: “Jesus, would You walk with me here?” He loves that prayer. Recognition may come slowly, but He is already beside you.

content.question: Where might Jesus already be present in my day—conversations, work, commute, meals—though I haven’t noticed Him yet?

content.text: Lord Jesus, draw near to me as I am. Teach me to slow my pace and listen for Your questions and comfort. Open my awareness to Your Presence in the ordinary moments of today. Help me trust that You walk with me even before I recognize You. Amen.
Choose one routine moment today (travel, dishes, break at work) and whisper: “Jesus, walk with me here.” Then notice one way you sense His nearness.

We often expect God to arrive with fireworks; He often arrives as a fellow traveler. Don’t despise the ordinary. The Lord of glory took a quiet road and a patient tone. If you feel unsure of how to spot Him, simply invite Him: “Jesus, would You walk with me here?” He loves that prayer. Recognition may come slowly, but He is already beside you.

steps.title: He Opens the Scriptures

content.text: Jesus doesn’t only comfort; He clarifies. He opens the Scriptures so our hearts can burn with living hope, not just warm feelings.

On the road, Jesus began to explain how the whole story of God points to Him. The Bible is not a box of inspirational quotes—it is a unified story that finds its centre in Christ. When Scripture is opened by Jesus, confusion loosens, burdens lift, and purpose emerges. For new believers, this is crucial: read the Bible not merely for advice but to meet the risen Lord. Ask, “What does this show me about who Jesus is and what He has done?” Over time you will discover that promises, patterns, and prophecies all converge on Him. Your heart may not blaze instantly, but steadily light grows as you return to the Word with Him as your Guide. Don’t be intimidated; start where you are. The same Jesus who walked those 11 kilometres delights to walk through Scripture with you, connecting the dots.

steps.title: Eyes Opened at the Table

content.text: Jesus meets us in Scripture and in simple, holy moments—like a shared meal. Recognition often comes where welcome and gratitude are present.

As evening fell, the disciples urged Jesus to stay. At the table, in the breaking of bread, their eyes were opened and they recognized Him. Notice the pattern: hospitality, gratitude, and fellowship become a doorway to revelation. The Christian life is not only about study and knowledge; it is tasted at the table—when we pause, give thanks, and make room for Jesus in our ordinary rhythms. Creating space for Him is powerful: a quiet corner to pray, a meal begun with gratitude, a conversation where you speak His Name with reverence. Recognition doesn’t depend on special effects; it grows where hearts are open and Jesus is welcomed. Let your table, your schedule, and your relationships become places where you say, “Stay with us.” He loves to reveal Himself where He is invited.

steps.title: Back to Jerusalem with Good News

content.text: When Jesus is revealed, our feet find a new urgency. The walk with God naturally overflows into witness—not from pressure, but from joy.

After recognizing Jesus, the two disciples immediately returned to Jerusalem to tell the others what had happened. This is the end and the beginning of the Emmaus Road: encountering the risen Christ sends us back into our world with a simple testimony—what we have seen and how our hearts burned as He opened the Scriptures. A relationship with God is a walk: He meets us in confusion, travels with us in conversation, opens His Word to us, reveals Himself in fellowship, and then propels us to share. You don’t need all the answers to witness; you need an honest story of how Jesus has met you. Joy is meant to be told. Ask God for one person to encourage today. Let your words be gentle, clear, and centered on Jesus. As you speak, remember: the same Lord who walked you to recognition now walks with you into mission.

steps.title: A Relationship, Not a Religion

content.text:
For some people, Christianity is mainly about religion.

Going to Church.

Following rules.

Believing certain things.

Trying to be a good person.

Those things may form part of someone's experience of Christianity, but Jesus invites us into something much deeper.

He invites us into a Relationship with God.

Think about the difference between knowing about someone and actually knowing them.

You can know someone's name.

Know where they live.

Know what they do.

Know things they've said.

And still not know them personally.

The same can happen with God.

We can know Bible stories.

Attend Church.

Sing Christian songs.

Understand Christian beliefs.

And still experience God mainly as someone we know about.

But from the beginning of this Journey, we've discovered something remarkable:

God wants to be known.

Jesus told His disciples that He called them friends.

Think about that.

The God who created everything invites ordinary people into Relationship with Him.

Christianity isn't humanity performing enough religious activities to keep God happy.

Through Jesus, we are invited to know God.

That Relationship will certainly change the way we live.

We'll learn God's Ways.

We'll obey Him.

We'll worship Him.

We'll gather with His people.

We'll serve others.

But those things grow out of Relationship.

They aren't a substitute for it.

Imagine a marriage where two people followed all the correct routines but never really spoke, listened, shared life or enjoyed one another's company.

Something important would be missing.

Relationship requires connection.

And Walking with God means learning to live connected to Him.

Not only during Church.

Not only while reading the Bible.

Not only when life becomes difficult and you desperately need help.

God invites you to walk with Him through ordinary life.

You can know Him.

God, thank You that You invite me into Relationship with You.

I don't want simply to know things about You or practise religion without knowing You.

Help me to know You more.

Teach me to recognise Your Presence, listen to Your Voice through Your Word, trust Your Character and enjoy walking with You.

Amen.

Ask yourself honestly:

Do I mostly know about God, or am I learning to know Him?

Don't judge yourself by your answer.

Simply talk to God about it.

Tell Him that you want to know Him more.

content.message: Well done! You have completed today's reading.

content.closingText:
God doesn't simply invite you to practise a religion.

He invites you to know Him.
content.lookingAhead:
Relationships grow when we learn to listen.

God hasn't left us guessing about who He is or how He wants us to live.

He has spoken.

Tomorrow we'll discover how we learn to listen to God through His Word.

steps.title: Listening to God

content.text:
If Walking with God is a Relationship, then we need to learn to listen.

Thankfully, God hasn't left us trying to guess what He thinks.

He has given us His Word.

People sometimes say:

"I wish God would speak to me."

Perhaps you've wondered the same thing.

How do I know what God wants?

How do I know what is true?

How do I know what God is actually like?

One of the most important answers is Scripture.

The Bible isn't simply a collection of ancient religious writings.

Through Scripture, God reveals His Character, His Ways, His purposes and the story of what He has done.

Paul tells Timothy that Scripture is God-breathed.

It teaches us.

Corrects us.

Trains us.

And equips us to live according to God's Ways.

That's why learning to read the Bible matters.

Not because reading a certain amount makes God love you more.

And not because Christians need another religious task to complete.

We open God's Word because we want to know the God who has spoken.

Sometimes Scripture will encourage you.

Sometimes it will comfort you.

Sometimes it will challenge something you're doing.

Sometimes you'll read something you don't understand.

That's okay.

You don't have to understand the entire Bible before you can begin listening.

Keep reading.

Keep learning.

Ask questions.

And allow Scripture to shape your understanding of God rather than expecting God to fit whatever you already believe.

There's also an important safeguard here.

We sometimes have thoughts, feelings or impressions and wonder whether God is speaking to us.

Those things should never be allowed to replace Scripture.

God will not guide us in a way that contradicts His Word.

The more familiar we become with Scripture, the better we learn to recognise God's Character and God's Ways.

Walking with God means becoming someone who listens.

And one of the primary ways we listen is by opening His Word.

God, thank You for giving me Your Word.

Give me a desire to know Scripture and wisdom to understand what I read.

Help me not simply look for verses that agree with what I already want, but allow Your Word to shape me.

Teach me to recognise Your Character, Your Truth and Your Ways through Scripture.

Amen.

When you open Scripture, try beginning with a simple prayer:

God, help me to hear what You want me to understand.

Then read slowly.

Ask:

What does this show me about God?

What does this show me about the way He calls me to live?

content.message: Well done! You have completed today's reading.

content.closingText:
You don't have to guess what God is like.

He has given us His Word.

Learn to listen.
content.lookingAhead:
A Relationship doesn't grow through listening alone.

God invites you to speak too.

Tomorrow we'll discover that Prayer isn't about finding impressive religious words.

It's simply learning to talk with God.

steps.title: Talking with God

content.text:
Some people find Prayer intimidating.

They hear other people pray and think:

I wouldn't know what to say.

But Jesus never intended Prayer to become a performance.

Prayer is part of your Relationship with God.

When Jesus taught His disciples to pray, He gave them what we now call the Lord's Prayer.

It shows us that Prayer can include many things.

We honour God.

We desire His Will.

We ask Him for what we need.

We ask for forgiveness.

We forgive others.

We ask for His help when we're tempted.

But Prayer isn't limited to repeating certain words.

Prayer is conversation with God.

You can thank Him.

Ask Him questions.

Tell Him when you're worried.

Admit when you're angry.

Confess when you've sinned.

Ask for wisdom.

Pray for someone you love.

Bring your disappointment to Him.

Sit quietly in God's Presence.

You don't need religious vocabulary.

You don't have to pretend everything is fine.

God already knows you.

Prayer is an invitation to come honestly into His Presence.

There may be times when Prayer feels natural.

There may also be seasons when you don't know what to say.

That's okay.

Relationship isn't measured by how impressive your words are.

Jesus also warned against turning Prayer into a performance designed to impress other people.

God isn't looking for impressive speeches.

He wants you.

So talk to Him.

In the car.

At home.

At work.

When you wake up.

When something wonderful happens.

When something goes terribly wrong.

When you need wisdom before making a decision.

Walking with God means learning to bring God into the conversation of your everyday life.

Father, thank You that I can talk to You.

Teach me to pray honestly.

Help me to bring You my gratitude, my needs, my fears, my failures and my questions.

Forgive me when I choose my own way.

Help me to recognise Your Presence throughout my day and learn to speak with You naturally.

Amen.

Talk to God today without trying to sound religious.

Tell Him what's actually happening in your life.

Something you're grateful for.

Something you're worried about.

Something you need help with.

Start there.

content.message: Well done! You have completed today's reading.

content.closingText:
Prayer isn't about impressing God with your words.

It's about learning to talk with the God who already knows you.
content.lookingAhead:
Listening to God and talking with Him deepen our Relationship.

But eventually Relationship asks for trust.

Tomorrow we'll explore what it means to trust God enough to follow His Ways.

steps.title: Trusting and Obeying God

content.text:
Trust is easy when God's Way agrees with ours.

The real test comes when it doesn't.

Walking with God means learning to trust that He knows what is good, even when His Way challenges our own.

Earlier in this Journey, we went back to the Garden of Eden.

Humanity faced a question:

Can God be trusted?

Adam and Eve chose their own way instead of God's Way.

In many ways, we still face that same question.

God says something through His Word.

We understand what He wants.

But another way seems easier.

More attractive.

More comfortable.

Or simply more like what we want.

What do we do?

Jesus connects love for Him with obedience.

That doesn't mean we earn His love by obeying enough rules.

Remember everything we've already discovered.

Jesus loved us while we were still sinners.

He went to the Cross for us.

Salvation is Grace.

We don't obey so that Jesus will love us.

We learn to obey because we trust the One who already does.

Obedience is where Faith becomes practical.

It's one thing to say:

"I trust God."

It's another to trust Him with your relationships.

Your money.

Your sexuality.

Your forgiveness of someone who hurt you.

Your integrity when nobody is watching.

Your ambitions.

Your habits.

Your future.

There will be times when God's Way costs you something.

That's when trust becomes real.

And when you fail, don't run away from God.

Come back.

Confess it.

Receive His Grace.

Learn from it.

Keep walking.

Walking with God isn't a lifetime of never making another mistake.

It's a lifetime of increasingly learning to say:

God, I trust Your Way more than mine.

God, help me to trust You.

There are times when my way feels easier than Yours.

Remind me that You are good and that Your Ways come from Your Character.

Help me obey You not because I'm trying to earn Your love, but because I trust You.

And when I fail, help me return to You quickly and keep walking.

Amen.

Ask yourself:

Is there an area where I already know God's Way but I'm struggling to trust Him enough to follow it?

Bring that area honestly to God.

Ask Him for the courage to take the next faithful step.

content.message: Well done! You have completed today's reading.

content.closingText:
Obedience isn't how you earn God's love.

It's what grows as you learn to trust the God who already loves you.
content.lookingAhead:
You've learned to listen.

To talk with God.

To trust.

To follow.

But Walking with God isn't something you do for a few days.

It's a lifetime.

Tomorrow we finish Come and See with one simple invitation:

Keep walking.

steps.title: Keep Walking

content.text:
You began Come and See with questions.

Perhaps you still have some.

That's okay.

Following Jesus doesn't mean reaching a point where every question disappears.

It means knowing who you're walking with.

Paul writes:

"Just as you received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to live your lives in him."

Continue.

That's an important word.

The Christian Life isn't one moment followed by instant spiritual maturity.

It's a journey.

You will learn.

Grow.

Change.

Discover.

There will be moments when you feel incredibly close to God.

There may be other times when God seems quiet.

There will be prayers that are answered in ways that amaze you.

There may be prayers where you struggle to understand His answer.

There will be victories.

There will be struggles.

There may be times when you stumble badly.

Keep walking.

Not because your Faith depends upon your ability to perform perfectly.

But because Jesus is faithful.

Keep opening God's Word.

Keep talking with Him.

Keep gathering with His people.

Keep learning to trust His Ways.

Keep responding when the Holy Spirit shows you something that needs to change.

Keep receiving Grace when you fail.

steps.title: The Choice to Trust God

content.text:
Before we talk about sin, we need to understand what existed before it.

God created humanity in His image.

He gave them a place to live, purpose and everything they needed.

And then God gave them something else:

A choice.

At the heart of that choice was a simple question.

Will you trust Me?

God placed Adam in the Garden of Eden and gave him responsibility to care for it.

He was free to enjoy what God had created.

There was abundance.

Freedom.

Purpose.

Relationship with God.

But there was also one boundary.

God told Adam not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

Why put the tree there at all?

Because genuine relationship involves trust.

God didn't create human beings as machines programmed to obey Him.

He gave humanity the ability to make real choices.

And with that freedom came responsibility.

Adam and Eve could trust that their Creator knew what was good for them.

Or they could decide that they knew better.

That's important because sin didn't begin simply with someone eating the wrong piece of fruit.

Something deeper was happening.

The question was:

Can God be trusted?

That's still one of the most important questions we face.

God's ways sometimes place boundaries around our lives.

There are things He tells us are good.

Things He warns us against.

Ways He calls us to live.

And sometimes we may wonder:

"Why shouldn't I?"

"What's wrong with it?"

"Why does God get to decide?"

"Wouldn't I be happier doing things my own way?"

Those questions take us right back to the garden.

God's boundaries weren't given because He wanted to keep something good from humanity.

They came from the God we've already been discovering—the Creator who is good, loving, holy and trustworthy.

Obedience to God was meant to grow out of trust in God.

That helps us understand what is about to happen in the story.

Humanity's first great failure wasn't simply breaking a rule.

It was choosing not to trust the One who gave the rule.

And if we're honest, that's a struggle we still recognise.

We often want God's goodness...

while still wanting the freedom to decide for ourselves what is right and wrong.

God, You created me and You know what is good for me.

Help me to trust Your character, especially when I don't fully understand Your ways.

Show me the areas where I want Your blessings but still insist on doing things my own way.

Teach me to trust that Your boundaries aren't intended to harm me, but come from Your wisdom and goodness.

Amen.

Consider this question honestly:

Do I trust God enough to let Him tell me what is good?

Think about the areas where trusting God comes easily—and the areas where you would rather make your own decisions.

You don't need to pretend.

Bring those places honestly to God.

content.message: Well done! You have completed today's reading.

content.closingText:
The first question in the garden wasn't really about fruit.

It was about trust.

Would humanity trust the God who created them?
content.lookingAhead:
The boundary was clear.

But another voice was about to enter the conversation.

A voice that suggested:

Maybe God can't be trusted.

Tomorrow we'll see what happened when humanity believed that voice and chose its own way.

And everything changed.
